conditions: For stomach ache that is suitable for home management and has no concerning warning signs.
recommendations: Sip water.
Avoid solid food for a few hours.
Avoid coffee, carbonated drinks, alcohol, spicy foods, fried foods and fatty foods.

conditions: When further advice is needed to manage symptoms.
When advice about suitable medication is required.
When unsure whether a GP or Emergency Department visit is necessary.
recommendations: Consult a pharmacist for advice on managing symptoms.
A pharmacist can recommend suitable medication or advise whether medical attention is needed.

conditions: Condition gets worse or does not improve within two weeks.
Fever of 38°C or higher.
Diarrhoea persists for more than two days.
Vomiting persists for a few hours.
Difficult or painful swallowing.
Severe pain.
recommendations: Seek medical assessment from a GP.

conditions: Sudden and severe abdominal pain.
Sweating and breathlessness.
Vomiting that does not subside.
Blood in vomit.
Bloody or black sticky stools.
recommendations: Go to the Emergency Department.

description: Bruises are caused by bleeding from injury to blood vessels beneath the skin.

conditions: For bruises that are suitable for home management and do not have concerning warning signs.
recommendations: Apply a cold compress to reduce swelling.
Elevate the bruised area above the level of the heart to reduce swelling.
Over-the-counter medications such as Paracetamol or Ibuprofen may be used to relieve pain.
Speak to a pharmacist if unsure how to take medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions or are taking other medications.

conditions: When further advice is needed to manage the bruise.
When advice about suitable medication is required.
When unsure whether a GP or Emergency Department visit is necessary.
recommendations: Consult a pharmacist for advice on managing the bruise.
A pharmacist can recommend suitable medication or advise whether medical attention is needed.

conditions: Severe pain from the bruise.
Pus draining from the bruise.
Red painful streaks around the bruise.
Fever.
Multiple unexplained bruises over the body.
Bruised area increases in size.
recommendations: Seek medical assessment from a GP.

conditions: Painful swelling of the bruised site affecting movement, which may indicate a fracture.
recommendations: Go to the Emergency Department.

description: Colds are usually mild and people normally recover on their own with little self-treatment. Influenza or flu can be more severe and contagious than a common cold.

conditions: For cold or flu symptoms that are suitable for home management and do not have concerning warning signs.
recommendations: Stay home and get plenty of rest.
Take a warm bath to help relax and soothe body aches.
Drink plenty of fluids.
Apply mentholated or vapour rubs to the chest, neck and back to help with breathing, especially before sleeping.
Over-the-counter medications such as Paracetamol, Ibuprofen and antihistamines may be used where appropriate.
Speak to a pharmacist if unsure how to take medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions or are currently taking other medications.

conditions: When further advice is needed to manage cold or flu symptoms.
When advice about suitable medication is required.
When unsure whether a GP visit is necessary.
recommendations: Consult a pharmacist for advice on managing symptoms.
A pharmacist can recommend suitable medication or advise whether medical attention is needed.

conditions: Condition gets worse or does not improve within two weeks.
Fever of 38°C or higher.
Cough with thick yellow or green phlegm.
Cough containing blood.
Difficulty breathing.
Age 65 or above with multiple long-term medical conditions.
Pregnancy.
Long-term medical conditions such as asthma, lung disease, heart disease, diabetes or kidney disease.
recommendations: Seek medical assessment from a GP.
MOH states that a cold or flu alone does not normally require an Emergency Department visit unless advised by a GP.

description: Cuts are wounds where the skin is lacerated or torn. Open wounds are caused by injury to the skin and may result in scarring or infection.

cuts.description: Cuts occur when the skin is lacerated or torn. Deep cuts may cause bleeding.

open_wounds.description: Open wounds are injuries to the skin that may result in scarring or infection.

conditions: For cuts and open wounds that are suitable for home management and do not have concerning warning signs.
recommendations: Clean the cut by rinsing it under clean water or normal saline.
Apply an appropriate dressing and firm pressure to the wound to stop bleeding if necessary.
Use sterile gauze swabs to clean the wound.
Swipe gently outward from the wound area, using a new swab for each swipe.
Use the corner of the swab to gently lift foreign material out of the wound.
Carefully pat the area dry with a clean gauze swab.
Apply a plaster or bandage.
For open wounds, wash with clean water or normal saline as soon as possible to remove dirt and debris.
Apply a non-adherent dressing to open wounds.
Keep open wounds clean and review them daily for signs of infection.

conditions: When further advice is needed to manage the wound.
When advice about suitable medication is required.
When unsure whether a GP or Emergency Department visit is necessary.
recommendations: Consult a pharmacist for advice on managing the wound.
A pharmacist can recommend suitable medication or advise whether medical attention is needed.

conditions: Visible dirt or foreign material, such as a splinter, remains inside a cut after washing.
The cut is caused by an animal or rusty object.
The cut shows no signs of improvement after more than one week.
Signs of infection such as fever, persistent redness, pain, swelling or pus.
The person was bitten by an animal.
The person was cut by a rusty object and has not received a tetanus booster within the last five years.
The open wound shows no signs of improvement after more than one week.
recommendations: Seek medical assessment from a GP.

conditions: A cut is deep and bleeding does not stop.
An open wound is deep and bleeding does not stop.
Fat or deeper structures such as tendon, muscle or bone are visible in the wound.
A foreign body is suspected in the wound.
Painful swelling of a limb affects movement, which may indicate a fracture.
recommendations: Go to the Emergency Department.

description: Vomiting is the forced emptying of the stomach through the mouth. Diarrhoea is the frequent passage of liquid stools. Both commonly occur together due to infections of the gut.
possible_causes: Side effects of certain medications, such as antibiotics

conditions: Symptoms can be managed at home when there are no warning signs requiring medical attention.
recommendations: Drink more water or clear fluids, such as clear soups, to prevent losing too much water.
Avoid foods that may worsen diarrhoea, such as coffee, alcohol, spicy foods, fried foods, fatty foods, and dairy products like milk and cheese.
Do not take solid food until vomiting has stopped.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing symptoms.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing diarrhoea and vomiting.
A pharmacist may recommend over-the-counter medications such as charcoal or oral rehydration salts.
Ask the pharmacist how to take medication safely, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions, or are currently taking other medications.
A pharmacist can advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Condition gets worse or does not improve in a few days.
Vomiting affects your ability to eat and drink.
High fever of 38°C and above persists for more than 3 days.
Recently travelled to countries with poor sanitation.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if any of the listed conditions apply.

conditions: Severe stomach pain.
Severe dehydration, such as feeling very thirsty, giddy, and weak.
Blood in vomit.
Bloody or black sticky stools.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: Vomiting is the forced emptying of the stomach through the mouth. Diarrhoea is the frequent passage of liquid stools. Both commonly occur together due to infections of the gut.
possible_causes: Side effects of certain medications, such as antibiotics

conditions: Symptoms can be managed at home when there are no warning signs requiring medical attention.
recommendations: Drink more water or clear fluids, such as clear soups, to prevent losing too much water.
Avoid foods that may worsen diarrhoea, such as coffee, alcohol, spicy foods, fried foods, fatty foods, and dairy products like milk and cheese.
Do not take solid food until vomiting has stopped.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing symptoms.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing diarrhoea and vomiting.
A pharmacist may recommend over-the-counter medications such as charcoal or oral rehydration salts.
Ask the pharmacist how to take medication safely, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions, or are currently taking other medications.
A pharmacist can advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Condition gets worse or does not improve in a few days.
Vomiting affects your ability to eat and drink.
High fever of 38°C and above persists for more than 3 days.
Recently travelled to countries with poor sanitation.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if any of the listed conditions apply.

conditions: Severe stomach pain.
Severe dehydration, such as feeling very thirsty, giddy, and weak.
Blood in vomit.
Bloody or black sticky stools.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: For most adults, a temperature of 37.5°C and above is considered a fever. Fever is usually a symptom of an illness, such as flu, overheating, dehydration, or sometimes an infection.

conditions: Fever without warning signs requiring medical attention.
recommendations: Use a thermometer to measure your temperature.
Drink plenty of water to stay hydrated.
Rest in a cool and airy room whenever possible.
Sponge yourself with lukewarm water.
Do not use ice water or cold water for sponging.
Do not sponge for more than 30 minutes at a time, as this may cause shivering and raise body temperature.
Over-the-counter medications such as paracetamol or ibuprofen may be used to treat fever.
Speak to a pharmacist if you are unsure how to take medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions, or are currently taking other medications.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing fever symptoms or medication.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing fever.
A pharmacist may recommend suitable medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Fever is 38°C and above even after taking over-the-counter medications.
Fever lasts more than 3 days.
You are pregnant.
You have recently returned from overseas.
You are taking medications that suppress the immune system.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if any of the listed conditions apply.

conditions: Difficulty in breathing, especially in children.
Chest pain.
Severe headache.
Severe back or neck pain.
Coughing with blood.
Pain when urinating.
Itchy skin rashes over the whole body.
Fits or seizures, such as the body shaking spasmodically, becoming rigid with the back arched, clenched jaw, or eyes rolling upwards.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: Feeling pain or pressure in the head is very common. Headaches can have various causes, ranging from everyday factors to more serious illnesses.

conditions: Headache without warning signs requiring medical attention.
recommendations: Get more sleep and rest.
Over-the-counter painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen may be used to treat headaches.
Speak to a pharmacist if you are unsure how to take medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions, or are currently taking other medications.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing headache symptoms.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing headache symptoms.
A pharmacist may recommend other medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Headache lasts for more than one day, even after taking over-the-counter pain relievers.
Headaches occur frequently, more than 15 days in a month.
Pain or throbbing is so strong that you cannot go about your daily routine.
Headache develops after a head injury, such as falling.
You are experiencing nausea or vomiting.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if any of the listed conditions apply.

conditions: Headache accompanied by a stiff neck.
Headache accompanied by confusion.
Headache accompanied by weakness or numbness in the limbs.
Headache accompanied by blurred vision.
Headache accompanied by difficulty speaking.
Headache accompanied by fits or seizures, such as the body shaking spasmodically, becoming rigid with an arched back, clenched jaw, or eyes rolling upwards.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if a headache occurs with any of these warning signs.

description: Hypertension is also known as high blood pressure. It is commonly caused by increased salt intake and ageing. Rarely, it may occur due to a stroke.

conditions: Managing existing high blood pressure without emergency warning signs.
recommendations: Continue taking regular antihypertensive medications as prescribed.
Avoid excessive salt intake in your diet.
Exercise regularly.
Get plenty of rest.

conditions: Blood pressure readings are consistently higher than usual.
Giddiness.
Headache.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if any of the listed conditions apply.

conditions: Weakness and/or numbness.
Difficulty seeing.
Difficulty speaking.
Difficulty walking.
Chest pain.
Shortness of breath.
Severe giddiness.
Severe headache.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: Hives are raised, itchy rashes that appear on the skin. They can affect one part of the body or cover large areas.
possible_causes: Allergic reactions to substances or chemicals

conditions: Hives without warning signs requiring emergency medical attention.
recommendations: Avoid scratching or rubbing the rashes, as this may worsen itching or redness.
Move to a cool room to work or sleep.
Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel to the affected areas.
Wear light and loose-fitting clothes.
Over-the-counter allergy medication such as antihistamines can be used to treat hives.
Speak to a pharmacist if you are unsure how to take medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions, or are currently taking other medications.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing hives.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing symptoms.
A pharmacist may recommend other medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Hives persist or worsen after a few days.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if hives persist or worsen after a few days.

conditions: Swelling of the eyes, lips, tongue, or throat.
Difficulty breathing.
Difficulty swallowing.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: Insect bites and stings usually cause minor irritation, such as swollen, itchy, red marks on the skin that last for a few days. Some bites and stings can be painful or trigger more serious allergic reactions.
possible_causes: Allergic reactions to insect bites or stings
symptoms: Pain around the bite or sting

conditions: Minor insect bites or stings without signs of infection or serious allergic reaction.
recommendations: If a stinger is present, gently scrape it off using your fingernail or the edge of a card.
Do not pinch the stinger with your fingers or use tweezers, as this may spread the venom.
Wash the bite with soap and water, then pat it dry.
Place an ice pack wrapped in a towel on the affected area.
Avoid scratching the bite, as this may cause an infection.
Over-the-counter allergy medication such as antihistamines can help relieve itching and swelling.
Paracetamol or ibuprofen can help relieve pain.
Speak to a pharmacist if you are unsure how to take medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions, or are currently taking other medications.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing symptoms.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing insect bites and stings.
A pharmacist may recommend other medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Signs of infection, such as fever, persistent redness and pain, swelling, or pus forming in the wound.
Previous allergic reaction to an insect bite or sting.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if signs of infection develop.
Seek assessment from a GP if you have previously experienced an allergic reaction to an insect bite or sting.

conditions: Multiple insect stings.
Stung in the mouth.
Stung in the throat.
Stung near the eyes.
Difficulty breathing.
Pain, itching, or swelling on other parts of the body.
Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhoea following a bite or sting.
Fast heart rate.
Giddiness.
Confusion or agitation.
Pale skin.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.
Treat symptoms of a serious allergic reaction as an emergency.

description: Burns and scalds are injuries to the skin caused by heat. Burns are caused by dry heat, such as fire or a clothes iron. Scalds are caused by liquids, steam, or chemicals. Both can be painful and may cause blisters or red, black, or charred skin.
possible_causes: Contact with a hot clothes iron

conditions: First-degree burns on a small area.
Second-degree burns on a small area.
recommendations: Remove clothing or jewellery near the burnt area.
If clothing is stuck to the wound, cut around it but do not remove the stuck fabric.
Pour cool water over the wound for at least 10 minutes.
Do not use ice, iced water, butter, or other greasy substances on the burn.
Loosely cover the burn with a sterile gauze bandage or cling wrap.
Do not touch the burn or burst any blisters.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing the burn or wound.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing the wound.
A pharmacist may recommend medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: The wound shows no signs of improvement after more than one week.
Signs of infection, such as fever, persistent redness and pain, swelling, or pus forming in the wound.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if the wound does not improve after more than one week.
Seek assessment from a GP if signs of infection develop.

conditions: Burns in the mouth.
Burns in the throat.
Burns involving the eyes.
Burns involving the ears.
Burns involving the genital area.
Burns covering a large area of the body, larger than the person's hand.
Burns caused by chemicals.
Burns caused by electricity.
Burns caused by lightning.
Third-degree burns, where the burnt skin is white, leathery, or charred.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: Nosebleeds occur when tiny blood vessels in the nose burst. Bleeding can come from one or both nostrils, may be heavy or light, and can last from a few seconds to over 10 minutes.
possible_causes: Irritation from foreign objects in the nose

conditions: Nosebleed without emergency warning signs.
recommendations: Sit down and lean forward.
Using your thumb and index finger, pinch the nose just above the nostrils.
Breathe through your mouth.
Continue pinching until the bleeding stops, usually after 10 minutes.
If the bleeding continues, hold for another 10 minutes and suck on some ice cubes.
If your nose is injured, place an ice pack wrapped in a towel on the bridge of your nose.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing nosebleeds.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing symptoms.
A pharmacist may recommend other medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Nosebleeds recur for no apparent reason.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if nosebleeds repeatedly occur without an obvious cause.

conditions: Nosebleed does not stop after 20 minutes.
Nosebleed is caused by an injury to the nose, such as being hit in the face by a fist or object.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if the nosebleed does not stop after 20 minutes.
Seek emergency assessment if the nosebleed is caused by an injury to the nose.

description: Cellulitis or skin infections are caused by bacterial infections and can result in painful, red, warm, and swollen skin.
possible_causes: Bacterial infection entering the body through broken skin.

conditions: Preventing skin infections and reducing the risk of cellulitis.
recommendations: Keep your skin clean.
Avoid scratching your skin, as broken skin allows bacteria to enter the body.
Control diabetes, as people with diabetes have a higher risk of infections.
Wear proper footwear, as ill-fitting footwear increases the risk of abrasions and ulcer formation.

conditions: Painful, red, warm, and swollen skin.
You have diabetes.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if you have painful, red, warm, and swollen skin.
People with diabetes should seek assessment from a GP according to the MOH guidance.

conditions: High fever and chills.
Severe pain.
Painful blisters.
Rapid progression of swelling.
Painful swelling of joints that affects movement.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if any of these warning signs occur.

description: Sore eyes, commonly known as conjunctivitis, is the inflammation of the thin layer of tissue covering the front of the eye, called the conjunctiva.
symptoms: Feeling like there is sand in the eye
Sticky coating on the eyelashes, usually when waking up

conditions: Sore eyes without warning signs requiring medical attention.
recommendations: Avoid touching or rubbing the affected eye.
Wash your hands frequently with soap and water.
Do not share towels or pillows with others.
Remove eye discharge using clean tissue paper or cotton wool soaked in water.
Do not wear eye makeup or contact lenses until symptoms clear up.
Hold a warm, damp cloth over your eyelids to relieve discomfort.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing sore eye symptoms.
recommendations: Ask a pharmacist for advice on managing symptoms.
A pharmacist may recommend other medications or advise whether you need to see a GP or visit the emergency department.

conditions: Condition gets worse or does not improve in 3 days.
Pain in the eye.
Pus discharge from the eye.
recommendations: Seek assessment from a GP if symptoms worsen or do not improve within 3 days.
Seek assessment from a GP if there is eye pain or pus discharge.

conditions: Sore eyes caused by chemical exposure.
Affected vision, such as blurred vision.
Sensitivity to light.
recommendations: Go to the emergency department if sore eyes are caused by chemicals.
Seek emergency assessment if vision is affected or there is sensitivity to light.

description: A strain is the stretching or tearing of muscles or tendons, while a sprain is the stretching or tearing of ligaments. Both injuries commonly occur during physical activities or accidents involving movement.
possible_causes: Physical activities that stretch or tear muscles, tendons or ligaments

injury_types.strain: Stretching or tearing of muscles or tendons. Commonly affects the legs and back.
injury_types.sprain: Stretching or tearing of ligaments around joints. Commonly affects the knees, ankles and wrists.

conditions: Strain or sprain symptoms that can be managed with home treatment
recommendations: Stop the activity that caused the injury immediately.
Follow PRICE therapy:
Protect the injured area.
Rest the injured area.
Apply an ice pack wrapped in a towel for 15 to 20 minutes.
Compress the injured area with an elastic bandage until the swelling stops.
Elevate the injured area above heart level, especially at night.
Over-the-counter oral pain medications such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, or pain relief creams or patches, may be used to relieve pain.
Speak to a pharmacist if unsure how to use medication, especially if you have allergies, other medical conditions or are taking other medications.

conditions: Further advice is needed on managing strain or sprain symptoms
recommendations: Seek advice on managing symptoms.
The pharmacist may recommend other medications.
The pharmacist can advise whether a GP visit or emergency department visit is needed.

conditions: Severe pain or swelling
Numbness or coldness in the injured area
The injured limb looks crooked or has unusual lumps
Unable to move the injured joint or muscle
Unable to put weight on the injured limb
Symptoms have not improved after 3 days of home treatment
recommendations: Visit a GP for medical assessment if any of these conditions occur.
The MOH advises that there is no need to visit the A&E for a strain or sprain unless a GP advises it.
